## Introduction

Partition was not a single decision but a forty-year accumulation. It began with the colonial decision to represent Indians as religious blocs, hardened into a claim of separate nationhood after 1940, was confirmed at the ballot box in 1946, and was executed with extraordinary haste in 1947. Tracing that sequence shows why each step narrowed the range of options available at the next.

## Stage 1 — Institutional Foundation (1906–1935)
- The All India Muslim League was founded at Dacca in 1906; the Indian Councils Act, 1909 granted separate electorates. The consequence was structural — from that point a Muslim politician's career depended on Muslim votes alone, so communal appeal became the rational electoral strategy. The Lucknow Pact (1916) briefly produced Congress–League unity, but by accepting separate electorates the Congress conceded the principle it would later have to fight. The Communal Award (1932) and the Government of India Act, 1935 carried the arrangement into full provincial autonomy.

## Stage 2 — Ideological Articulation (1930–1940)
- Iqbal's Allahabad address (1930) envisaged a consolidated Muslim north-west; the Lahore Resolution of 23 March 1940 formally demanded independent States in the Muslim-majority zones. Jinnah's Two-Nation Theory supplied the justification — that Muslims constituted a nation, not a minority. The significance of this stage is that it changed the currency of negotiation from safeguards to sovereignty, rendering every subsequent federal proposal structurally inadequate.

## Stage 3 — Electoral Confirmation (1937–1946)
- In 1937 the League performed poorly among Muslim voters; Congress's refusal of coalition in the United Provinces pushed it towards mass communal mobilisation and the "Day of Deliverance" of 1939. Congress ministries resigned in 1939 over the war declaration, leaving the field to the League. In the 1945–46 elections the League swept the reserved Muslim seats, winning all thirty in the Central Assembly. It could now claim, with electoral authority, to be the sole spokesman of Indian Muslims — which is precisely what gave it a veto over every subsequent plan.

## Stage 4 — Constitutional Breakdown (1942–1946)
- Cripps (1942) conceded a provincial right of non-accession — the first British admission of the possibility of partition. The Gandhi–Jinnah talks (1944) and the Simla Conference (June 1945) foundered on the League's claim to nominate all Muslim members. The Cabinet Mission Plan (May 1946) offered a united India with grouping; when the Mission clarified that grouping was compulsory, the League withdrew acceptance on 29 July and called Direct Action Day for 16 August 1946. The Great Calcutta Killings, Noakhali, Bihar and the Punjab followed. Violence, not argument, ended the debate.

## Stage 5 — Legal Execution (1947)
- Attlee announced on 20 February 1947 that Britain would leave by June 1948; Mountbatten arrived on 24 March, judged the situation irretrievable, and advanced the date. The 3 June Plan provided for partition of Bengal and the Punjab, a referendum in the NWFP and Sylhet, and separate Constituent Assemblies.
- The Indian Independence Act, 1947 received assent on 18 July. The Radcliffe Boundary Commission's award, completed in about five weeks, was published only after independence. Pakistan came into being on 14 August and India on 15 August 1947.

## Conclusion

Partition was the cumulative product of institutional design, ideological escalation, electoral confirmation and administrative haste. Its human cost — the displacement of more than fifteen million people and mass killing across Punjab and Bengal — constituted one of the largest forced migrations in recorded history. The task of nation-building did not end on 15 August 1947: the integration of over five hundred princely States, completed in Hyderabad only in September 1948, was the unfinished second half of the same story. Partition continues to define India's northern and western frontiers and the strategic architecture of South Asia.

## Value addition
- Andhra Pradesh anchor: Partition did not divide the Telugu country, but its logic reached it through the princely State of Hyderabad. With paramountcy lapsing, the Nizam declined accession, the Razakars intensified, and integration came through Operation Polo on 17 September 1948. The Ministry of Home Affairs notified in March 2024 that 17 September will be observed annually as Hyderabad Liberation Day; the 2025 commemoration at Hyderabad's Parade Ground included a fifty-panel Central Bureau of Communication exhibition on Operation Polo.
- Official memory:Partition Horrors Remembrance Day, 14 August, instituted in 2021 and commemorated annually by IGNCA under the Ministry of Culture — the natural closing reference for this answer.
- Precision points that distinguish a script: Pakistan's Independence Day is 14 August, India's 15 August; the Radcliffe award was published after transfer of power; the Constituent Assembly's strength fell from 389 to 299.
- Andhra continuity: the Telugu districts' political energy in this period flowed into the linguistic States movement — Potti Sriramulu's fast unto death in December 1952 and the creation of Andhra State on 1 October 1953, the first State formed on a linguistic basis and the trigger for the States Reorganisation Commission.
- Sequence for revision: 1906 → 1909 → 1916 → 1932 → 1940 → 1942 → 1946 → 3 June 1947 → 18 July 1947 → 14–15 August 1947 → 17 September 1948.

## Introduction

Indian foreign policy between 1947 and 1989 was shaped by three inheritances — the memory of colonial subjection, the trauma of Partition, and a bipolar Cold War order. Article 51 of the Directive Principles gave it constitutional expression, enjoining the promotion of international peace, respect for international law and settlement of disputes by arbitration. What emerged was not passive neutrality but an active attempt to preserve freedom of judgement while lacking the material power normally required for it.

## Non-Alignment as Strategic Autonomy, Not Neutrality
- Nehru refused formal military blocs so that India could judge each issue on its merits — the term "non-alignment" was first used by V.K. Krishna Menon at the United Nations in 1953. The distinction from neutrality matters: India condemned the Anglo-French action at Suez in 1956 while its muted response to Hungary the same year exposed the policy's inconsistencies. Institutionally this ran from Bandung (1955) to the first Non-Aligned Summit at Belgrade (1961), giving newly decolonised States collective bargaining weight they individually lacked.

## Panchsheel and Principled Coexistence
- The Five Principles — mutual respect for sovereignty and territorial integrity, non-aggression, non-interference, equality and mutual benefit, and peaceful coexistence — were embodied in the India–China Agreement of April 1954. Their reach was genuinely global: they were expanded at Bandung in 1955, incorporated in a resolution on peaceful coexistence moved by India, Yugoslavia and Sweden and adopted unanimously by the UN General Assembly on 11 December 1957, and accepted as the principled core of NAM at Belgrade in 1961.

## The Neighbourhood and the Turn to Realism
- 1962 as the first correction: The Sino-Indian war exposed the gap between principle and preparedness. It produced sustained defence modernisation, a hardened border posture and the quiet abandonment of the assumption that shared anti-colonial sentiment guaranteed peace.
- 1971 as the second: Faced with roughly ten million refugees from East Pakistan, India signed the Indo-Soviet Treaty of Peace, Friendship and Cooperation in August 1971 to neutralise the US–China axis, intervened militarily, and then converted victory into the Simla Agreement (1972) — establishing bilateralism as the governing principle of the Kashmir question. Regional activism by the 1980s: SAARC was founded at Dhaka in 1985; the IPKF deployment in Sri Lanka (1987) and Operation Cactus in the Maldives (1988) showed India willing to act as a regional security provider — a considerable distance from 1950s moral suasion.

## Multilateralism, the Global South and the Nuclear Question
- India used the UN, the Commonwealth and NAM to press decolonisation, oppose apartheid and demand a New International Economic Order, and became a leading contributor to UN peacekeeping — converting moral standing into diplomatic leverage in the absence of hard power.
- On the nuclear question India refused the NPT in 1968 as discriminatory, conducted the "peaceful nuclear explosion" at Pokhran in 1974, and yet in 1988 Rajiv Gandhi presented an Action Plan for universal, time-bound nuclear disarmament at the UN. This deliberate ambiguity — capability retained, weaponisation deferred, disarmament advocated — is the clearest illustration of idealism and realism operating simultaneously.

## Economic Constraint as a Shaping Force
- A weak economic base restricted the instruments available. The 1965–66 food crisis and dependence on PL-480 wheat imports demonstrated how aid dependence could translate into diplomatic vulnerability, and pushed India towards the Green Revolution and towards a Soviet relationship offering defence supplies on rupee terms.

## Conclusion

By 1989 Indian foreign policy had travelled from moral idealism to calibrated realism without abandoning its founding purpose. The rhetoric of non-alignment persisted while the practice became increasingly hard-headed — but the constant beneath both was strategic autonomy, the refusal to subordinate national judgement to any external centre. The collapse of the Soviet Union and the balance-of-payments crisis of 1991 dissolved the framework within which that autonomy had been exercised, compelling the reorientation towards economic diplomacy and multi-alignment that defines Indian foreign policy today.

## Value addition
- Andhra Pradesh anchors:Visakhapatnam, headquarters of the Eastern Naval Command, was central to the 1971 war — the Pakistani submarine PNS Ghazi sank off Visakhapatnam harbour in December 1971, and the Eastern Fleet's operations enabled the naval blockade of East Pakistan. The Sriharikota range in Nellore district, established in 1971, became the platform for the technological self-reliance that underpinned strategic autonomy.
- Dr Sarvepalli Radhakrishnan, Telugu-speaking philosopher-statesman, served as India's first Ambassador to the USSR (1949– 52) and built the personal relationship that later matured into the 1971 Treaty; Neelam Sanjiva Reddy of Anantapur was President from 1977 to 1982 during the Janata-era recalibration of ties with China and the United States.

Q60:
## Introduction

The Satavahanas (c. 1st century BCE – 3rd century CE) and their successors the Ikshvakus of Vijayapuri (c. 3rd – early 4th century CE) together span the formative four centuries of Andhra's early historic culture. The transition between them is not a repetition but an evolution: a wide Deccan-scale, trade-driven, Prakrit-using order gives way to a compact Krishna-valley polity marked by deeper Sanskritisation, temple-building and international monastic contact.

1. Social composition: from open commercial society to entrenched hierarchy

- Satavahana society was varna-ordered but commercially mobile. Inscriptions name occupational groups — halika (cultivator), kolika (weaver), gandhika (perfumer), vasakara (bamboo-worker), tilapisaka (oil-presser) — whose shrenis made independent donations. That donative capacity is the proof of real economic autonomy, and many such crafts later hardened into castes.
- Royal ideology was itself hybrid: Gautamiputra Satakarni is styled Ekabrahmana yet also khatiya-dapa-mana-mardana ("crusher of the pride of Kshatriyas"), and the Nasik Prasasti claims he ended varna-samkara — a claim that betrays how fluid social boundaries actually were.
- Under the Ikshvakus, agrahara grants and a court of titled feudatories (mahatalavara, mahasenapati) narrowed this openness. Elite patronage replaced broad-based guild patronage as the dominant idiom of donation.

2. Religion: from plural patronage to a Brahmanical-Buddhist division of labour Satavahana kings performed Vedic sacrifices while endowing Buddhist establishments — the Naneghat record of Naganika lists dakshinas for Agnyadheya, Rajasuya and two Ashvamedhas, even as Nasik and Karle caves were being gifted to monks.

- The Ikshvakus formalised this: the kings themselves were Mahasena-Shiva devotees performing Ashvamedha, Vajapeya and Agnihotra, while the royal women endowed Buddhism. Chamtisri, sister of Chantamula I, built the Mahachaitya at Nagarjunakonda; Bodhisri's pillar inscription records gifts to fraternities from Tambapamnidipa (Sri Lanka), Kashmir, Gandhara, China, Aparanta, Vanavasa and the Yavana country.
- This is the analytical core: pluralism became gendered and institutionalised rather than merely tolerant, and Andhra Buddhism turned outward into an Indian Ocean network.

3. Language and learning: Prakrit to Sanskrit Satavahana official language was Prakrit in Brahmi; Hala's Gathasaptasati and Gunadhya's Brihatkatha (Paisachi) made it a literary medium and, uniquely, a window on village and women's life.

- Ikshvaku inscriptions retain Prakrit but admit increasing Sanskrit, and Nagarjunakonda became a monastic university associated with Acharya Nagarjuna and the Madhyamaka school — a shift from courtly poetry towards scholastic philosophy.

4. Art and architecture: narrative relief to iconic image and temple The Amaravati school under the Satavahanas used white-green limestone for dense narrative medallions and ayaka platforms, moving from aniconic symbols (Bodhi tree, footprints, wheel) to the Buddha image.

- The Nagarjunakonda school under the Ikshvakus is more plastic and naturalistic, absorbing Gandhara and Mathura idioms; alongside it appear the earliest brick Hindu shrines to Ashtabhujasvamin, Karttikeya and Shiva, plus a stone-built amphitheatre — the only one known from ancient India.

## Conclusion

The evolution was therefore one of deepening rather than reversal. The Satavahanas built a broad, mercantile, Prakrit-speaking Deccan culture; the Ikshvakus compressed it into the Krishna valley, gave it Sanskritic learning, temple form and an international monastic reach. Together they converted Andhradesa from a frontier named in Vedic texts into a recognised centre of the Buddhist world.

## Value addition
- Nagarjunakonda (Vijayapuri), named after the later Satavahana ruler Vijaya Satakarni, is protected by ASI; its island museum is built on a vihara plan, and the 1950s relocation of monuments before submergence by the Nagarjunasagar reservoir remains a landmark salvage operation in Indian archaeology (ASI / Museums of India portal, Ministry of Culture).
- Adarsh Smarak (Model Monument) status of ASI covers three Andhra sites — Nagarjunakonda's reconstituted monuments, the Buddhist remains at Salihundam, and the Virabhadra and Basava temples at Lepakshi.
- Andhra Pradesh's integrated Buddhist Heritage Circuit links Amaravati, Nagarjunakonda, Ghantasala, Adurru, Thotlakonda and Bavikonda; the Buddhist Circuit is a notified thematic circuit under the Ministry of Tourism's Swadesh Darshan scheme.
- Jainism under the Ikshvakus survived at Penugonda, Pithapuram, Nedunuru and Draksharamam; six Tirthankara images of the 3rd century CE are reported from Aryavatam.
- Exam-hall line: "Under the Satavahanas Andhra sent goods to the world; under the Ikshvakus it received monks from it."
Q61:
## Introduction

The Satavahanas filled the political vacuum left by the Mauryan collapse and ruled the Deccan for roughly four centuries. The Puranas call them Andhras or Andhra-bhrityas, though their own inscriptions never use the term — a discrepancy that lies at the root of a long debate about where their power actually began.

1. The origin debate — "trace" begins here The Western Deccan case rests on the earliest inscriptions being at Naneghat and Nasik and on Pratishthana (Paithan, Godavari) appearing as the capital, suggesting a Maharashtra origin with later eastward expansion.

- The Eastern Deccan case rests on the coin evidence from Kotilingala (Jagtial, Telangana) bearing the legend Chimuka Satavahana, alongside early sites at Dhulikatta, Peddabankur and Kondapur — arguing that the dynasty rose in the Telangana-Andhra tract and moved west.
- The Puranic king-lists compound the problem: the Matsya Purana gives thirty kings over 456 years, the Vayu about nineteen — figures that cannot all be reconciled, which is why chronology here is stated as a range, not a date.

2. Expansion Simuka founded the line; Kanha (Krishna) extended it to Nasik; Satakarni I conquered western Malwa and Berar and performed two Ashvamedhas and a Rajasuya, recorded with their dakshinas in the Naneghat inscription of his queen Naganika.

- Gautamiputra Satakarni (c. 106–130 CE) marks the zenith. The Nasik Prasasti of Gautami Balasri styles him destroyer of the Sakas, Yavanas and Pahlavas, uprooter of the Kshaharata line (Nahapana), and lord of Asika, Asaka, Mulaka, Surashtra, Kukura, Aparanta, Anupa, Vidarbha, Akara and Avanti — effectively the whole Deccan and its northern approaches.
- Vasishthiputra Pulumavi consolidated the east, with Amaravati and Dhanyakataka rising as centres; Yajna Sri Satakarni (c. 165– 194 CE), the last major ruler, issued ship-motif coins attesting active maritime trade before the dynasty fragmented before the Abhiras, Ikshvakus and Western Kshatrapas.

3. Contribution to religion The kings were Brahmanical in legitimation — Vedic sacrifices, gifts of thousands of karshapanas and cows to Brahmanas at Naneghat, Gautamiputra's title Ekabrahmana — and Buddhist in patronage, endowing the stupas at Amaravati, Bhattiprolu and Jaggayyapeta and the rock-cut chaityas of Karle, Nasik and Bhaja.

- They also gave Buddhism its Andhra character: the Mahasanghika sub-sects flourished in the Krishna valley, and the ayaka-platform stupa with limestone casing became a regional type exported to Sri Lanka and Southeast Asia.
- Jainism was tolerated, with rock-shelters of Jain ascetics reported at Munulagutta near Kotilingala.

4. Contribution to literature Hala's Gathasaptasati — seven hundred verses in Maharashtri Prakrit, a court anthology of rural and erotic lyric that is also our best social document of the period; tradition names several women among its contributors.

- Gunadhya's Brihatkatha in Paisachi Prakrit, a vast story-cycle now lost but surviving through the Sanskrit Kathasaritsagara — the fountainhead of Indian narrative literature.
- Acharya Nagarjuna, contemporary of Yajna Sri Satakarni, founded the Madhyamaka school; his Suhrllekha, a letter of counsel to the Satavahana king, was widely memorised, as the Chinese pilgrim I-tsing later noted.
- Correction: Nagarjunakonda's monastic university belongs to the Ikshvaku period, not the Satavahana; and the Kamasutra is more securely dated to the Gupta age. Do not present either as Satavahana achievements.

## Conclusion

The Satavahanas were the Deccan's first imperial builders and its first great cultural synthesisers. By simultaneously performing Vedic sacrifice and endowing Buddhist chaityas, and by making Prakrit a court literary language, they created a durable regional idiom of power. Andhradesa's later dynasties inherited that idiom, and the Amaravati stupa remains its most eloquent surviving statement.

## Value addition
- Prakrit received Classical Language status on 3 October 2024 (PIB / Ministry of Culture), taking the total to eleven Indian classical languages as of October 2025. Since Gathasaptasati and every Satavahana inscription are in Prakrit, this is the sharpest available current hook for a Satavahana literature question.
- Amaravati Mahachaitya: ASI dates the site from the 3rd century BCE to the 4th century CE. Most of its finest panels were removed in the colonial period to the Government Museum Chennai, the Indian Museum Kolkata and the British Museum; the relic caskets and remaining sculptures are in the ASI site museum (ASI Amaravati Circle).
- Digital access: Burgess's 1887 survey of the Buddhist stupas of Amaravati and Jaggayyapeta is available through the IGNCA's ASI digital collection — a citable primary-documentation source.
- Satavahana coinage: lead, potin, copper and silver with Brahmi-Prakrit legends; the ship-type coins of Yajna Sri are the earliest Indian numismatic evidence of a state advertising sea power.

## Introduction

The Ikshvakus of Vijayapuri emerged in the Krishna valley around the middle of the third century CE as the Satavahana empire fragmented, and ruled for barely three generations. Yet in that short span they turned Nagarjunakonda into one of the ancient world's great Buddhist centres, making theirs one of the most culturally consequential short dynasties in Indian history.

1. Political fortunes Vasishthiputra Chantamula, the founder, claimed Kshatriya status and descent from the epic Ikshvakus and performed Ashvamedha, Vajapeya and Agnihotra — ritual assertions typical of a feudatory house converting local power into sovereign legitimacy after imperial collapse.

- Mathariputra Virapurushadatta marks the peak, secured through marriage diplomacy: he married Ikshvaku princesses and Rudradhara-bhattarika, daughter of the ruler of Ujjain, tying the Krishna valley to the Western Kshatrapa world.
- Ehuvala Chantamula sustained the state and expanded temple-building; the last known ruler, Rudrapurushadatta, is attested by an inscription of the early fourth century, after which the Pallavas and Abhiras absorbed the territory.
- Vijayapuri, laid out on the Krishna with a citadel, planned streets and a fortified enclosure, was both capital and pilgrimage city — the political and the religious were deliberately fused.

2. Religion: a gendered division of patronage The kings were Brahmanical — devotees of Mahasena-Kartikeya and Shiva, performers of Vedic sacrifice, donors of agraharas — while the royal women endowed Buddhism, the single most distinctive feature of Ikshvaku religious life.

- Chamtisri, sister of Chantamula I, built the Mahachaitya at Nagarjunakonda in the sixth regnal year of Virapurushadatta; Bodhisri's pillar inscription records endowments for monastic fraternities from Tambapamnidipa (Sri Lanka), Kashmir, Gandhara, China, Aparanta, Vanavasa, Yavana and Damila lands — the clearest single proof of Andhra's place in an intercontinental Buddhist network.
- Buddhist sects named in the inscriptions — Aparamahavinaseliya, Bahusrutiya, Mahisasaka — show Nagarjunakonda hosting doctrinal diversity, not a single orthodoxy.

3. Art, architecture and language Over thirty monastic establishments were built at Nagarjunakonda — stupas with ayaka platforms, chaityagrihas, viharas — together with the earliest brick Hindu temples of the region to Ashtabhujasvamin, Karttikeya and Shiva, and a stone amphitheatre, the only structure of its kind known from ancient India.

- The Nagarjunakonda school of limestone sculpture developed the Amaravati manner into fuller, more naturalistic figures under Gandhara and Mathura influence, with narrative panels of Jataka scenes, donor processions and courtly life that double as social documents.
- Prakrit remained the language of record, but Sanskrit gained ground — Chantamula's sacrificial inscriptions are among the earliest Sanskrit epigraphs of the south, marking the linguistic turn that the Salankayanas and Vishnukundins would complete.

## Conclusion

Politically the Ikshvakus were a brief, regional and ultimately fragile power. Culturally they were anything but: they gave Andhra its most refined sculptural school, its earliest surviving Hindu temples, its first Sanskrit epigraphs and, through Bodhisri's endowments, a permanent place on the Buddhist map of Asia. Their short rule shows how decisively cultural investment can outlive political fortune.

All dates are approximate and derived from regnal years in inscriptions, not from an absolute era — say so rather than asserting precise figures.

Q63:
## Introduction

The Satavahanas (c. 1st century BCE – 3rd century CE) were the first indigenous imperial power to rise in the Deccan after the Mauryan collapse, welding the Krishna–Godavari doab into the political unit that ancient texts call Andhradesa. Their four centuries were not a static age but one of structural transition — from tribal formations to a monetised, guild-organised and religiously plural society, documented in the Naneghat and Nasik inscriptions, Hala's Gathasaptasati and Roman accounts.

1. Social conditions: a hierarchy that was formal but still permeable

- Varna upheld in theory, fluid in practice. Gautami Balasri's Nasik prasasti praises Gautamiputra Satakarni for halting the intermixing of the four varnas — yet the dynasty's own varna is disputed, called Sudra in the Puranas, Kshatriya-by-marriage in the Nasik record and of Naga descent in Kathasaritsagara. That such ambiguity survived at the very top proves ritual status was still negotiable in Andhra, unlike the settled Gangetic order.
- Occupation, not birth alone, defined the middle strata. Donative inscriptions name the ashtadasha (eighteen) crafts — kolikas (weavers), suvarnakaras (goldsmiths), tilapishakas (oil-pressers). These occupational guilds hardened into jatis only under the Eastern Chalukyas, which is precisely why Andhra's later caste map is craft-derived rather than purely scriptural.
- Women held real economic and ritual agency. Metronymics such as Gautamiputra and Vasishthiputra were adopted as dynastic titles; Naganika issued the Naneghat record and performed Vedic sacrifices; Gautami Balasri granted land in her own name. Against this, the Gathasaptasati records the loneliness of seafarers' wives and the presence of sati and prostitution — prosperity was unevenly distributed.

2. Economic conditions: technology, guilds and Indo-Roman trade

- An agrarian base deepened by grants and machinery. The Satavahanas introduced the first systematic land-grant system in South India, drawing forest and fallow under the plough; the ghatiyantra (water-lift) and girika (cotton gin) are among the earliest documented labour-saving devices in the peninsula, explaining how surplus large enough to fund Amaravati was generated.
- Guilds as the institutional core.Srenis pooled craft capital, acted as bankers and appear repeatedly as stupa donors; sarthavahas (caravan merchants) worked the Ujjain–Pratishthana–Dhanyakataka corridor. Commerce and religion were therefore not separate spheres but one financing circuit.
- Overseas trade with Rome. Pliny's Natural History and the Periplus of the Erythraean Sea record Andhra's exports of muslin, pearls, sandalwood and diamonds; Roman coins at Kondapur and rouletted ware at Salihundam corroborate them. Ports at Koddura, Ghantasala, Kottapatnam and Dharanikota, and the ship motif on Yajnashri Satakarni's lead coins, complete the picture.

3. Religious conditions: patronage without exclusivity

- Brahmanism was the court religion — Naganika's Naneghat inscription lists Ashvamedha and Rajasuya sacrifices with the dakshina paid, making it a rare fiscal record of ritual.
- Buddhism was the popular religion. Mahadeva Bhikshu's chaityakavada generated the five Saila sects (Purvasaila, Aparasaila, Uttarasaila, Rajagirika, Siddharthika) centred on Amaravati, Bhattiprolu, Jaggayyapeta and Gudivada; Acharya Nagarjuna's Suhrullekha was addressed to Yajnashri Satakarni, showing philosophy reaching the throne itself.
- Jainism survived on lighter patronage at Ramatirtham and Danavulapadu, with Kondakundacharya's Saraswatigachcha order — proof that pluralism was policy, not accident.

## Conclusion

The Satavahana centuries thus fused a permeable social order, a technologically improved and trade-driven economy, and a state that financed Brahmanical yajnas and Buddhist chaityas from the same treasury. This composite model — surplus underwriting pluralism — was inherited intact by the Ikshvakus at Vijayapuri and remains the earliest recognisable template of Andhra's regional civilisation. Model Question: "Satavahana prosperity was the fiscal foundation of Andhra's religious pluralism." Examine this statement with reference to guilds, maritime trade and monastic patronage.

Colonel Colin Mackenzie recorded the remains in 1797.

## Introduction

Under the Satavahanas (c. 1st century BCE – 3rd century CE), Andhradesa acquired both a plural religious culture and the first recorded traces of its language. The paradox of the age is that its official and literary medium was Prakrit, yet it is from precisely these Prakrit records — the Amaravati inscription and Hala's Gathasaptasati — that the earliest surviving Telugu words are recovered.

1. Socio-religious conditions: coexistence as state policy

- Dual patronage from a single treasury. Gautamiputra Satakarni is celebrated in the Nasik prasasti as a restorer of Brahmanical order, while the same dynasty funded the Amaravati and Bhattiprolu stupas. This was not indecision but statecraft: Brahmanism legitimised the throne, Buddhism bound the trading and artisanal classes to it.
- Monasteries as social institutions. Amaravati, Nagarjunakonda, Jaggayyapeta and Salihundam functioned simultaneously as pilgrimage centres, schools and rest-houses for caravans, which is why Buddhism spread fastest along Andhra's trade corridors rather than into its interior uplands.
- Donative agency of women and commoners. Inscriptions record gifts by nuns, merchants' wives and guilds alongside those of Naganika and Gautami Balasri. Buddhism's indifference to birth-status offered non-Brahmanical and tribal groups — Nagas, Pulindas — a route into public religious life that Vedic ritual did not.

2. Language: Prakrit as the medium, Telugu as the substratum

- Prakrit was the language of state and of literature. Every Satavahana inscription is in Prakrit, and Hala's Gathasaptasati — an anthology of 700 verses — marks its golden age. Gunadhya's Brihatkatha (Paisachi) and Kutuhala's Lilavati Parinayam belong to the same milieu.
- The first Telugu word is epigraphic, not literary. "Nagabu" occurs in the Amaravati inscription of Vasishthiputra Pulumavi — the earliest attested Telugu form. Its appearance inside a Prakrit record is the crucial evidence: Telugu was the spoken tongue of the donors even where the scribe wrote Prakrit.
- Literary Prakrit absorbed Telugu vocabulary.Gathasaptasati carries desi words such as atta, amma, addam, potta, pandi, pilla. A court anthology admitting village Telugu shows the language was already prestigious enough in daily use to leak upward.

3. Literature and learning: Sanskrit joins the mix

- Sarvavarman's Katantra Vyakarana and Vatsyayana's Kamasutra were composed for Kuntala Satakarni's court, while Acharya Nagarjuna and Aryadeva wrote Mahayana philosophy in Sanskrit — establishing the trilingual Prakrit–Sanskrit–Telugu environment from which Nannaya's classical Telugu would emerge eight centuries later.

## Conclusion

The Satavahana age was therefore Telugu's pre-literary phase: it produced no Telugu text, but it produced the conditions for one — a settled regional identity, a script, a donor class that spoke Telugu, and a literary culture confident enough to absorb desi vocabulary. Socio-religious pluralism and linguistic emergence were two faces of the same integration of Andhra's peoples. Model Question: "The Satavahana age gave Telugu its speakers, not its literature." Critically examine, with epigraphic and literary evidence, the emergence of Telugu under the Satavahanas.

## Value addition
- Telugu was conferred Classical Language status in 2008 by the Ministry of Culture. As of October 2025, India recognises 11 classical languages; Prakrit and Pali — the very media of Satavahana Andhra — were added in October 2024 (PIB).

4.40 lakh are publicly accessible on the Gyan Bharatam portal.

Q65:
## Introduction

Between the 3rd century BCE and the 4th century CE, Andhradesa was transformed from a frontier of Mauryan influence into one of the two great generative centres of Indian Buddhism. Its distinction was not merely the number of its stupas but that Andhra produced doctrine — the Mahasanghika schism, the Saila sects and Nagarjuna's Madhyamaka — and produced a sculptural idiom, the Amaravati school, that travelled across maritime Asia.

1. Why Buddhism took root: the social explanation

- Andhra's tribal groups — Nagas, Pulindas and others — stood outside the varna order and found in Buddhism a faith that assigned worth by conduct rather than birth. Buddhism thereby did politically what no dynasty had yet managed: it gave warring forest tribes one shared identity, easing the Satavahana task of governing a united Andhradesa.
- Buddhism suited a commercial society. Unlike Vedic ritual, it placed no stigma on trade or profit, so the merchant and artisan classes of the Krishna delta — the region's rising wealth — adopted it as their own.

## The trajectory of growth
- Mauryan contact: Ashoka's minor rock edicts at Erragudi and Rajula-Mandagiri (Kurnool) confirm imperial Buddhist presence in Rayalaseema by the 3rd century BCE; the Bhattiprolu caskets, with their distinctive early Brahmi, show relic worship already institutionalised.
- Doctrinal creativity: Mahadeva Bhikshu's chaityakavada at Amaravati precipitated the Mahasanghika split and generated the five Saila sects — Purvasaila, Aparasaila, Uttarasaila, Rajagirika and Siddharthika. Andhra was thus a source of Buddhist thought, not a recipient of it.
- Patronage across classes: Satavahana and Ikshvaku kings, Ikshvaku queens such as Chamtisri and Bodhisri, guilds and individual nuns all appear as donors. Acharya Nagarjuna, founder of Sunyavada, corresponded with Yajnashri Satakarni in the Suhrullekha — philosophy reaching the throne. Salihundam alone preserves all three yanas, Hinayana, Mahayana and Vajrayana.

## Salient features of Buddhist art and architecture
- The Andhra stupa type. ASI records the Amaravati Mahachaitya at roughly 50 m in diameter and 27 m high, with four rectangular Ayaka platforms (7.20 × 2.10 m) at the cardinal points, each bearing five Ayaka pillars for the five great events of the Buddha's life. This ayaka projection is the defining regional signature, absent at Sanchi and Bharhut.
- The Amaravati sculptural school. Executed in white-greenish limestone, it is marked by crowded narrative medallions of Jataka and life scenes, slender elongated figures in vigorous tribhanga, and a documented shift from aniconic symbols (Bodhi tree, footprints, dharmachakra) to iconic Buddha images. Bhattiprolu, Jaggayyapeta and Ghantasala share the idiom.
- Monastic and educational architecture. Nagarjunakonda–Vijayapuri combined mahachaitya, chaitya-grihas, viharas, an amphitheatre and planned drainage; the Anupu complex, identified by ASI as a university establishment with separate quarters for female disciples, shows monasticism organised as formal education.

## Conclusion

Andhra's Buddhist achievement was therefore threefold: it integrated the region's peoples, it generated original doctrine, and it created an artistic language of its own. The Ayaka stupa and the Amaravati idiom travelled to Sri Lanka and Southeast Asia, and the region's monks — Nagarjuna, Buddhaghosa, Padmasambhava — carried Andhra's learning across Asia, giving the Telugu country its first identity of global consequence. Model Question: "Andhra was not a periphery of Indian Buddhism but one of its generative centres." Evaluate this claim with reference to doctrinal developments and the Amaravati school of art.

## Introduction

Founded when Kubja Vishnuvardhana I, brother of Pulakesin II of Badami, declared independence at Vengi in c. 624 CE, the Eastern Chalukya dynasty ruled the Krishna–Godavari delta for roughly five centuries until 1130 CE. Their significance is not measured in conquests but in continuity: they held Andhra together through the transition from the ancient to the early medieval age, and in doing so gave the Telugu country its first durable political and cultural identity.

## Political significance
- They created Andhradesa as a geographical expression. Their empire brought coastal Andhra, Rayalaseema and parts of Telangana under a single authority for the first time, converting a cultural label into a political unit — the precondition for every later Andhra polity from the Kakatiyas to the Reddis.
- They functioned as a buffer state. Positioned between the Rashtrakutas and Kalyani Chalukyas to the north-west and the Cholas to the south, Vengi absorbed the shock of peninsular rivalry. Their longevity, despite being weaker than both neighbours, is itself the evidence of skilled equidistant diplomacy.
- Matrimonial diplomacy converted subordination into succession. Kundavai, daughter of Rajaraja Chola I, married Vimaladitya of Vengi; Rajaraja Narendra married Ammangadevi, daughter of Rajendra Chola I. Their son ascended the Chola throne in 1070 as Kulottunga I — an extraordinary outcome in which the junior partner's line inherited the senior empire.
- They completed administrative and monetary consolidation, issuing gold madas and gadyanas alongside silver and copper coin, standardising a currency system that the Kakatiyas would inherit — a quiet but decisive contribution to Andhra's commercial integration.

## Role in moulding Andhra culture
- They gave Telugu its script and its literary metres. The progression is traceable inscription by inscription: the Vipparla record of Jayasimha carries the earliest Telugu prose; Panduranga's Addanki inscription introduces the taruvoja metre; the Kandukur inscription yields sisapadya; and Yuddhamalla II's Bezawada inscription the madhyakkara. Telugu acquired a written prosody before it acquired literature.
- They launched classical Telugu literature. Under Rajaraja Narendra (c. 1022–1061 CE), Nannaya Bhattaraka began the Andhra Mahabharatamu and composed the grammar Andhra Sabda Chintamani, earning the title Adikavi. Tikkana and Errapragada later completed the epic, giving Telugu a Sanskritic diction on a Dravidian base.
- They created Andhra's temple idiom. The Pancharama shrines — Draksharama, Samalkota (Kumararama), Amaravati, Palakollu and Bhimavaram — together with the Biccavolu group, fused Chalukyan structure with Dravidian articulation, establishing the model the Kakatiyas would refine at Palampet.
- They institutionalised learning and the arts.Ghatikas and agraharas at Bezawada, Ramatirtham, Rajahmundry and Amaravati taught grammar, logic, medicine and astronomy; the dancer Chellava, honoured by Chalukya Bhima with the title Gana-Gandharva-Visarada, indicates court patronage of music and dance.

## Conclusion

The Vengi Chalukyas were architects rather than conquerors. Politically they gave Andhra a unified territory, a durable buffer diplomacy and a monetised administration; culturally they gave it a script, a metrical tradition, a first epic and a temple style. When the Kakatiyas rose at Warangal, they did not begin afresh — they inherited an Andhra that the Eastern Chalukyas had already made coherent. Model Question: "The Eastern Chalukyas survived not by strength but by diplomacy, and endured not through conquest but through culture." Critically evaluate this assessment of the Vengi kingdom.

## Introduction

The Eastern Chalukyas of Vengi (c. 624–1130 CE), ruling from Vengi and later Rajamahendravaram, presided over Andhra's first cultural renaissance. Standing between the Deccan Chalukyan north and the Chola south, they did not merely borrow from both — they synthesised a distinct Andhra idiom in script, metre, epic poetry and temple form that later Telugu dynasties treated as their inheritance.

1. Literature: from inscription to epic

- The pre-literary inscriptional stage is the real foundation. Telugu's poetic apparatus was assembled in stone before it appeared in manuscript: the Vipparla record of Jayasimha preserves the earliest Telugu prose; Panduranga's Addanki inscription introduces the taruvoja metre; the Kandukur inscription the sisapadya; and Yuddhamalla II's Bezawada inscription the madhyakkara. Without these, Nannaya would have had no prosody to work in.
- Nannaya Bhattaraka and the birth of classical Telugu. Court poet of Rajaraja Narendra (c. 1022–1061 CE), Nannaya rendered the Mahabharata into Telugu — completing the Adi and Sabha parvas and beginning the Aranya — and wrote the grammar Andhra Sabda Chintamani. He is titled Adikavi, the first poet, and his method fixed Telugu's enduring register: Sanskrit diction carried on Dravidian syntax.
- The tradition he opened was completed by others. Tikkana and Errapragada finished the epic; Nannechoda's Kumarasambhavamu pioneered the jaanu Telugu (pure Telugu) style that Palkuriki Somanatha would take further, while Pavuluri Mallana produced a Telugu mathematical work, Ganitasarasangrahamu — evidence that vernacular writing extended into technical knowledge, not devotion alone.

2. Architecture: the Pancharama and Biccavolu idiom

- The Pancharama Kshetras are the dynasty's signature. Chalukya Bhima I built the Bhimeswara temples at Draksharamam and Samalkota (Kumararama) between roughly 892 and 922 CE; with Amararama at Amaravati, Ksheerarama at Palakollu and Somarama at Bhimavaram, these five constitute Andhra's oldest continuously worshipped Saiva network.
- The distinguishing form is the two-storeyed, fortress-like plan. Draksharamam has two prakarams, the outer pierced by four gopura entrances, with a monolithic Spatika linga rising through the upper floor — a vertical arrangement rare in South Indian temple design and reproduced at Samalkota.
- Biccavolu shows the stylistic fusion clearly. Its group of shrines, built in the 9th–10th centuries in Dravidian style, combines Chalukyan structural massing with Chola-influenced articulation and niche sculpture — the visual definition of Vengi's intermediate position.

## Art, sculpture and the cultural apparatus
- Sculptural panels narrate Ramayana and Mahabharata episodes and carry mature icons of Shiva, Vishnu, Surya and Devi — the Panchayatana concept — while bilingual Telugu and Sanskrit inscriptions on temple walls make these buildings the principal epigraphic archive of the period.
- The temple was also an educational institution. Attached ghatikas, agraharas and mathas at Rajahmundry, Bezawada and Amaravati taught grammar, logic, medicine and astronomy, sustained by royal land grants; the dancer Chellava, titled Gana-Gandharva-Visarada by Chalukya Bhima, attests to court patronage of the performing arts.

## Conclusion

The Eastern Chalukyas converted Telugu from a spoken tongue into a literary language, and Andhra from a frontier of two architectural traditions into a region with a style of its own. Nannaya's epic and the Pancharama temples are not isolated achievements but the two halves of a single cultural programme, which the Kakatiyas at Palampet and the Reddis at Kondavidu inherited and elaborated. Model Question: "Telugu acquired its metres in stone before it acquired its poetry in manuscript." Discuss the contribution of Eastern Chalukya inscriptions and court patronage to the birth of classical Telugu literature.

Q68:
## Introduction

The Eastern Chalukyas of Vengi, founded by Kubja Vishnuvardhana in 624 CE after Pulakesin II's Deccan campaign, ruled the Krishna–Godavari doab for over four centuries until Vengi merged into the Chola realm in 1070 CE. Their significance for Andhra is not military but civilisational. By endowing schools, temples and poets, they converted a spoken Dravidian tongue into a written literary language, and gave the Telugu country its first self-conscious cultural identity.

## Contribution to education
- Agraharas and ghatikas as endowed institutions. The Chalukyas granted revenue-free villages (brahmadeya, agrahara) to scholars, where Veda, Vedanga, vyakarana, nyaya and jyotisha were taught. The reason this mattered is structural: because the grant carried its own revenue, learning did not depend on an annual royal budget and therefore survived war, succession disputes and the 1070 merger intact.
- Temple as college. The Bhimeswara temple at Draksharamam (Konaseema district), built by Chalukya Bhima I (c. 892–921 CE), functioned simultaneously as shrine, school and record office; its walls carry hundreds of inscriptions registering endowments for teachers, reciters and feeding houses. Pithapuram and Samalkot show the same pattern.
- A graded scholarly hierarchy. Titles such as Bhatta, Pandita and Somayaji appear in Rajaraja Narendra's grants, showing examination-linked ranks rather than informal teaching — the precondition for a poet like Nannaya to emerge from a trained class.

## Cultural contribution
- Managed religious plurality. Saivism dominated, but Vaishnavism, Jainism and residual Buddhism were all endowed. The Pancharama Kshetras — Amararama (Amaravati), Draksharama, Somarama (Bhimavaram), Ksheerarama (Palakollu) and Kumararama (Samalkot) — were consolidated in this period, creating a pilgrimage circuit that knitted coastal Andhra into a single sacred geography.
- A distinct sculptural idiom. The Golingeswara group at Biccavolu (East Godavari, ASI-protected) preserves 9th-century

Ardhanarisvara, Surya and Ganesha panels in which Chalukyan mass is blended with Rashtrakuta modelling and Chola proportion — visual proof that Vengi absorbed rather than resisted its powerful neighbours.

- Bilingual epigraphic culture. Chalukya charters run in Sanskrit for eulogy and Telugu for the operative grant. This division of labour is the first documentary sign of Telugu being treated as a language of record, not merely of speech.

## Contribution to Telugu language and literature
- Telugu enters verse before it enters literature. The Addanki inscription of Pandaranga (c. 848 CE, Prakasam district) in taruvoja metre and the Bezawada inscription of Yuddhamalla II in madhyakkara show metrical Telugu already in public use two centuries before Nannaya — a point that lifts an answer above the ordinary.
- Nannaya Bhattaraka and the Andhra Mahabharatam. Commissioned by Rajaraja Narendra, Nannaya — assisted by Narayana Bhattu — rendered two and a half parvas in the champu form, mixing verse and prose. The choice of the Mahabharata was deliberate: translating the most authoritative Sanskrit text was the fastest way to claim equal dignity for Telugu.
- Standardisation and succession. The grammar Andhra Sabda Chintamani is traditionally ascribed to him, and his diction and metre set norms that Tikkana (under Manumasiddhi II of Nellore) and Errana (under Prolaya Vema Reddy of Kondavidu) worked within, completing the epic and forming the Kavitrayam.

## Conclusion

The Eastern Chalukyas converted political stability into cultural capital. Their agraharas institutionalised learning, their temples at Draksharamam and Biccavolu fused regional and imperial idioms, and their patronage of Nannaya gave Telugu a written classical form. When Vengi's independence ended in 1070, its institutions did not: the Kakatiyas, Reddis and Vijayanagara rulers inherited a functioning literary language and a trained scholarly class. That inheritance, more than any conquest, is the Vengi legacy.

Q69:
## Introduction

Between 1000 and 1500 AD, Telugu moved from an inscriptional and spoken medium into a full literary language with settled grammar, metre and genres. The change was driven by three successive patronage systems — Vengi Chalukya, Kakatiya and Reddi–Vijayanagara — and by the Bhakti movement, which supplied both audience and idiom. But the growth was uneven: it began as a court monopoly, and its later reach owed as much to devotional dissent as to royal favour.

Phase I: Foundation under the Eastern Chalukyas, 11th–12th centuries

- Nannaya and Narayana Bhattu rendered two and a half parvas of the Mahabharata for Rajaraja Narendra (1019–61 CE) in the champu form. Its importance is that it created a prestige register: Telugu could now do what Sanskrit did, and the aristocracy had a reason to read it.
- Nannechoda's Kumarasambhavam, written in the Pakanadu region outside the Vengi court, shows a non-royal, desi-leaning stream running from the very beginning. The booklet's single-track story misses this.

Phase II: The desi and Virasaiva turn, 12th–13th centuries

- Palkuriki Somanatha composed Basava Purana and Panditaradhya Charitra in the dvipada couplet. The metrical choice is the argument: dvipada is easy to sing and memorise, so the work could reach cultivators and artisans who could not follow champu. This is Telugu's first mass literature.
- Tikkana Somayaji, minister at Nellore under Manumasiddhi II, wrote Nirvachanottara Ramayanam and Parvas 4–18 of the epic, and his invocation to Hari-Hara-natha made literary form carry a message of Saiva–Vaishnava reconciliation at a time of sectarian friction.

Phase III: Maturity under the Reddis and Vijayanagara, 14th–15th centuries

- Errana completed Nannaya's abandoned Aranya Parva under Prolaya Vema Reddy of Kondavidu, closing the Kavitrayam. He also wrote Harivamsam and Nrisimha Puranam.
- Srinatha, honoured as Kavisarvabhauma at the Kondavidu court of Pedakomati Vema Reddy, produced Sringara Naishadham, Kasikhandam and Bhimakhandam — and, in Palnati Veeracharitra, turned local Palnadu history into epic, showing Telugu could narrate its own past, not only Sanskrit's.
- Potana's Andhra Mahabhagavatamu was dedicated to Rama rather than to a king — a deliberate refusal of court patronage that marks literature's growing independence. Annamacharya, from 1424, poured devotional sankirtanas at Tirumala into everyday Telugu set to music.

## Critical evaluation
- Access was narrow at the top and broad only through bhakti. Champu literature required Sanskrit competence; the genuinely popular corpus is dvipada and sankirtana. Growth in prestige and growth in reach came from opposite directions.
- Sanskritisation created its own problem. Heavy tatsama loading opened the grandhika–vyavaharika gap that would remain unresolved until Gurajada and Gidugu in the 20th century.
- Women are almost absent until Tallapaka Timmakka and Molla in the 15th century, and the surviving canon is overwhelmingly coastal Andhra and Rayalaseema.
- The "golden age" label flattens the politics. The 14th century was one of Sultanate incursion and dynastic collapse; literary flowering happened despite, and partly because of, that disorder, as displaced courts competed for cultural legitimacy.

## Conclusion

Between 1000 and 1500 AD Telugu acquired grammar, metre, genre range and a canon, and by 1500 it was administratively and devotionally embedded across Andhradesa. But the achievement was double-tracked: courts gave it dignity while bhakti gave it people. Judged critically, the period produced not one golden age but a productive tension between elite and popular Telugu — a tension that shaped the language for the next four centuries.

## Value addition
- The Kalamalla inscription (Kamalapuram, YSR Kadapa district, c. 575 CE) of Erikal Muturaju Dhanunjaya is regarded as the earliest full Telugu inscription; the Addanki inscription (Prakasam district, c. 848 CE) is the earliest in Telugu verse — the epigraphic base on which the 1000–1500 literary edifice was built.
- Telugu received Classical Language status on 31 October 2008 (Ministry of Culture); the criteria include high antiquity of texts over 1,500–2,000 years, an original literary tradition, and knowledge texts and epigraphic evidence beyond poetry. Total classical languages now stand at 11 after the Cabinet decision of 3 October 2024 (PIB).

- Gyan Bharatam Mission (Central Sector Scheme, 2024–31, ₹482.85 crore) covers survey, documentation and digitisation of over one crore manuscripts, including palm-leaf Telugu kavya manuscripts held in AP mathas and private collections (PIB, Ministry of Culture).

## Introduction

Atukuri Molla, traditionally placed in the Vijayanagara period, is the best-known woman poet of medieval Telugu and the first from an artisan caste to enter its canon. Daughter of a potter of Gopavaram in the Kandukur region of present SPSR Nellore district, she composed the Molla Ramayanam and dedicated it to Sri Kantha Malleswara of Srisailam. Her importance lies in a double breach — of caste and of gender — achieved not by protest but by writing better, and plainer, than her contemporaries.

## Life and social location
- Caste and craft. Molla was the daughter of Atukuri Kesana, a Kummara (potter) and a devotee of Srisaila Mallikarjuna. In a canon populated by Brahmin court poets and royal patrons, an artisan woman authoring a full kavya is an event, not an anecdote.
- Self-taught, and openly so. She describes herself as unlettered in formal sastra and credits the grace of Srisailam for her verse. This was not false modesty but a strategy: divine sanction supplied the legitimacy that a guru-lineage would otherwise have provided, and it made her exclusion from formal learning an argument rather than a handicap.
- Geography matters for APPSC. Gopavaram (SPSR Nellore) and Srisailam (Nandyal district) place her squarely in Andhra Pradesh's Rayalaseema–Nellore devotional corridor, at a time when the literary centre of gravity was the Vijayanagara and Kondavidu courts.

2. Her work: the Molla Ramayanam

- Compression as artistry. The poem follows Valmiki's narrative across six kandas, ending with Rama's coronation and omitting the Uttara Kanda — and therefore Sita's second exile. Whether or not the omission was deliberate, its effect is to leave Sita's dignity intact, and examiners reward candidates who notice this.
- Selective emphasis. The Sundara Kanda receives fuller treatment than its proportion warrants, reflecting its independent devotional popularity in the Telugu country.
- Not a translation but a retelling. She reorganises and abridges freely rather than rendering the Sanskrit line by line, which is why the work reads as an original Telugu kavya rather than a derivative.

## Style
- Achcha Telugu. She composed in native Telugu vocabulary, keeping Sanskrit tatsama and long compounds to a minimum. The consequence is direct: her verses are intelligible to a listener with no Sanskrit, which is exactly the audience the court poets did not write for.
- Her own test of poetry. She held that a verse which is not understood the moment it is heard is useless — comparable, in her image, to a conversation between two people who can neither speak nor hear. Style, for her, is an ethical position about who literature belongs to.
- Prasada and dhara. Clarity and flow rather than ornament; simple metres, short compounds, everyday similes drawn from domestic and rural life.

## Conclusion

Molla's achievement is that she made accessibility a literary standard rather than a concession. By composing a compact Ramayana in Achcha Telugu, dedicating it to a deity rather than a king, and centring Sita's dignity, she demonstrated that neither Sanskrit learning nor court patronage was a precondition for excellence. She stands with Tallapaka Timmakka at the head of a slender but decisive line of Telugu women poets, and her Ramayana remains in household recitation five centuries on.

## Value addition
- The Centre of Excellence for Studies in Classical Telugu (CESCT) now functions from Venkatachalam Mandal, SPSR Nellore district — Molla's own district — after relocation from CIIL Mysuru under State G.O. No. 246 of 13-04-2022; it runs the Bhasha Sanchika classical Telugu portal (CIIL, Ministry of Education).
- Telugu holds Classical Language status conferred by the Ministry of Culture on 31 October 2008; India's classical languages now number 11 following the Union Cabinet decision of 3 October 2024 (PIB).
- Srisailam (Nandyal district), to whose deity Molla dedicated her work, is both a Jyotirlinga and a Shakti Peetha — the only site combining both — and remains one of Andhra Pradesh's principal pilgrimage economies.
- Palm-leaf manuscripts of regional Ramayanas fall within the Gyan Bharatam Mission (Central Sector Scheme 2024–31, ₹482.85 crore), which aims to survey and digitise over one crore manuscripts; the National Mission for Manuscripts has digitised about 3.5 lakh so far (PIB, Ministry of Culture).
- Molla, Tallapaka Timmakka (wife of Annamacharya, author of Subhadra Kalyanam) and, later, Tarigonda Vengamamba form the recognised line of Telugu women poets — a useful three-name spine for any women-in-literature question.
Q71:
## Introduction

Between 1000 and 1565 AD, Telugu was transformed from an inscriptional medium into a classical literature with a settled canon, from Nannaya's Mahabharatam to the prabandhas of Krishnadevaraya's court. Within that expansion, a small but significant number of women entered authorship — Tallapaka Timmakka, Molla, and arguably Mohanangi. Evaluating the period therefore means asking not only how far Telugu travelled, but who was allowed to travel with it.

## The mainstream trajectory, in brief
- Kavitrayam. Nannaya (with Narayana Bhattu) under Rajaraja Narendra; Tikkana under Manumasiddhi II of Nellore; Errana under Prolaya Vema Reddy of Kondavidu — three courts across three centuries completing one epic, which itself demonstrates the durability of the literary institution.
- The Reddi interlude.Srinatha, Kavisarvabhauma at Kondavidu, and Potana, whose Andhra Mahabhagavatamu was dedicated to Rama rather than a patron, extended range from epic to devotional and local-historical narrative.
- Vijayanagara peak. The Ashtadiggajas — Allasani Peddana (Manucharitramu), Nandi Timmana (Parijatapaharanamu), Dhurjati, Pingali Surana, Tenali Ramakrishna and others — perfected the prabandha. Krishnadevaraya's own Amuktamalyada made a Tamil woman saint, Goda Devi, the heroine of a Telugu imperial poem.

2. Women poets: the core of the answer

- Tallapaka Timmakka (c. mid-15th century), wife of Annamacharya, composed Subhadra Kalyanam in dvipada and is the earliest Telugu woman poet whose work survives. Her route to authorship was the household workshop: the Tallapaka family at Tirumala was a multi-generation literary establishment, so a wife could write without institutional schooling. This is the single most important mechanism of women's authorship in the period.
- Atukuri Molla, a potter's daughter of Gopavaram in present SPSR Nellore district, wrote a compact Ramayanam in Achcha Telugu and dedicated it to Sri Kantha Malleswara of Srisailam rather than to a king. Her route was bhakti: devotion supplied the sanction that caste and gender denied. She is the point at which the caste ceiling, not merely the gender ceiling, is breached.
- Mohanangi, daughter of Krishnadevaraya, is credited with Marichi Parinayam — attribution is debated, but it indicates royal women as authors and not only as patrons. Flag the debate rather than asserting it.
- Gangadevi, wife of Kumara Kampana, wrote Madhura Vijayam narrating the Vijayanagara recovery of Madurai (c. 1371) — but in Sanskrit. She is the instructive contrast: elite women's writing still gravitated to Sanskrit, and the Telugu shift is what makes Timmakka and Molla historically significant.

## Evaluation
- Access came through devotion and family, not institutions. No agrahara or ghatika admitted women; every known woman author writes from either a literary household or a bhakti sanction. The pattern explains both the achievement and its scale.
- It was exceptional, not systemic. Four or five names across five and a half centuries do not constitute a movement. An honest evaluation says the period produced remarkable individuals within an unchanged structure.
- The record is biased by survival. Oral and dvipada compositions by women were less likely to be copied onto palm leaf and endowed for preservation, so the surviving canon almost certainly understates women's participation.
- Nonetheless the direction is real. By 1565, a potter's daughter's Ramayana circulated alongside imperial prabandhas — something inconceivable in Nannaya's Vengi.

## Conclusion

Between 1000 and 1565 AD, Telugu achieved a complete classical apparatus — grammar, metre, genre and canon — and by the close of the period it was the language of both imperial poetry and village recitation. Women's entry into that literature was narrow but decisive: Timmakka through the household, Molla through devotion. Their contribution is best evaluated not by volume but by demonstration — they proved that Telugu authorship required neither Sanskrit schooling nor high caste, and the later tradition, down to Tarigonda Vengamamba, built directly on that proof.

- The CESCT operates from Venkatachalam Mandal, SPSR Nellore district, AP under CIIL, Ministry of Education, and has published Teluguvari Sasanalu on Telugu epigraphy.

- Krishnadevaraya's Amuktamalyada, composed in Telugu though he was a Tuluva by descent, is both a prabandha on a woman saint and a treatise on statecraft — usable in history, literature and polity answers alike.

## Introduction

Nannaya Bhattaraka, court poet of the Eastern Chalukya king Rajaraja Narendra (1019–1061 CE) at Rajamahendravaram, is honoured as Adikavi and Vaganusasanudu, the first poet and the law-giver of speech. Assisted by Narayana Bhattu, he rendered two and a half parvas of the Mahabharata into Telugu and, in doing so, converted a language that had appeared only in inscriptions and songs into a vehicle of high literature. Estimating his contribution means measuring both what that act created and what it foreclosed.

## The textual achievement
- The Andhra Mahabharatam. Nannaya composed the Adi and Sabha parvas and part of the Aranya parva — two and a half of eighteen — in the champu form mixing metrical verse with rhythmic prose.
- Why the Mahabharata. The choice was strategic, not accidental. Rendering the most authoritative Sanskrit text was the quickest possible demonstration that Telugu could carry philosophical, legal and narrative weight; nothing less prestigious would have settled the question.
- An unfinished monument. That he stopped mid-parva became productive: it gave Tikkana and Errana a defined task, and the eventual completion by three poets across three dynasties turned the epic into a shared national project of the Telugu country rather than one court's ornament.

## The linguistic intervention
- Grammar. The Andhra Sabda Chintamani, a Sanskrit-language grammar of Telugu, is traditionally ascribed to him, though modern scholarship disputes it. Either way, his practice functioned as grammar: later poets treated his usage as normative, which is why the title Vaganusasanudu stuck.
- Script and orthography. His work belongs to the moment when the Telugu–Kannada script of the Chalukya charters was settling into recognisably Telugu forms, giving the written language a stable visual identity.
- Lexical policy. He admitted Sanskrit tatsama vocabulary freely while retaining Telugu syntax and case structure. This created a hybrid literary register capable of abstraction — the single most consequential decision in Telugu literary history.

## The stylistic legacy
- His verse advertises three qualities that later criticism treats as his signature: lucid narration, euphonic beauty of syllable, and richness of meaning. These became the standard against which Telugu poetry was judged for five hundred years.
- He fixed the marga (classical, Sanskrit-derived) tradition as the prestige mode, with the champu form and Sanskrit metres such as utpalamala and champakamala as its default vehicles.

## The estimate
- On the credit side, he created a prestige register where none existed, made the Mahabharata a Telugu possession, and set diction, metre and narrative norms stable enough to survive three dynastic collapses.
- On the debit side, the heavy Sanskritisation placed literature beyond the unlettered, and the court-commission model tied it to royal favour. Both limitations produced their own correction: the desi counter-current of Nannechoda's Kumarasambhavam and Palkuriki Somanatha's dvipada Basava Purana arose precisely against the register Nannaya established.
- Net estimate. Nannaya's contribution was foundational rather than complete. He did not give Telugu its whole literature; he gave it the standard that everything afterwards — including the reaction against him — had to define itself against. That is the strongest form of influence a first poet can have.

## Conclusion

Nannaya's two and a half parvas did more for Telugu than many complete works have done for other languages. He supplied a literary register, a metrical vocabulary and a normative usage, and he attached them to the most authoritative narrative available. His Sanskritised idiom carried real costs in accessibility, and the desi poets soon said so — but they said so in a literary Telugu that only Nannaya had made possible. On any fair estimate, he remains the necessary starting point of the tradition.

## Value addition
- Adikavi Nannaya University at Rajamahendravaram (Rajahmundry), East Godavari district — the seat of Nannaya's patron Rajaraja Narendra — is Andhra Pradesh's institutional memorial to the poet, and the district still carries the name Rajamahendravaram.
- Telugu received Classical Language status from the Ministry of Culture on 31 October 2008; the criteria include high antiquity of early texts over 1,500–2,000 years and epigraphic and prose evidence beyond poetry. India's classical languages now number 11 after the Cabinet decision of 3 October 2024 (PIB).
- The Centre of Excellence for Studies in Classical Telugu, relocated to Venkatachalam Mandal, SPSR Nellore district, AP (G.O. No. 246 of 13-04-2022), publishes on classical Telugu grammar and inscriptions, including Teluguvari Sasanalu (CIIL, Ministry of Education).
- Gyan Bharatam Mission — Central Sector Scheme 2024–31, outlay ₹482.85 crore — targets over one crore manuscripts including palm-leaf copies of the Andhra Mahabharatam and its commentaries; roughly 3.5 lakh manuscripts already digitised under NMM (PIB, Ministry of Culture).
- The Addanki inscription of Pandaranga (c. 848 CE, Prakasam district) in taruvoja metre proves metrical Telugu was in public use nearly two centuries before Nannaya — useful for arguing that he formalised rather than invented literary Telugu.

## Introduction

The Kakatiyas (c. 1083–1323) unified the Telugu-speaking country for the first time under a single sustained authority, extending from Orugallu across Velanadu to the Krishna–Godavari coast. Their socio-economic order rested on an unusual combination — large-scale artificial irrigation in the dry interior joined to a deliberately protected maritime trade on the coast — and it was this combination that funded a mobile, service-based social structure.

## Water engineering as the foundation of the agrarian order
- Tank cascades at Pakhal, Laknavaram and Ramappa converted forest and scrub into wet cultivation. Because tanks were built chiefly by chiefs and temples rather than by the state alone, tank-building became the standard route by which a local family converted wealth into recognised social standing.
- Land was graded as wet, dry and garden, with the share taken varying accordingly — a calibrated system that permitted remission in years of failure, which inscriptions record.

## Trade, ports and the Abhaya Sasanam
- The Motupalli Abhaya Sasanam (1244–45 CE) of Ganapatideva ended the customary seizure of shipwrecked cargo and promised foreign merchants security of person and goods against a fixed, moderate duty. Its importance is conceptual: the Kakatiyas grasped that predictable taxation yields more than plunder — an early articulation of commercial trust as state policy.
- The policy worked. Marco Polo, visiting during Rudramadevi's reign, records Mutfili's diamonds and its remarkably fine cotton cloth. Textiles, diamonds from the Krishna valley, iron and spices moved to Southeast Asia; the charter's model was copied a century later by the Reddi ruler Anavota Reddi at the same site.

## Social mobility through the nayankara service tenure
- Land assigned in return for military service allowed non-aristocratic groups — Velamas, Reddis, Kammas and Padmanayakas — to convert soldiering into landed status. The Kakatiya polity was thus less a closed caste order than an open service order in which arms and irrigation both bought rank.
- Coastal chiefly houses were incorporated rather than crushed: the Kota chiefs of Dharanikota retained position under Kakatiya suzerainty, and Jayapa Senani of the Ayya family of Divi island in the Krishna delta became a Kakatiya commander and governor of Velanadu — and wrote the Nritta Ratnavali, the classic treatise that records desi dance forms including Perini.
- Rudramadevi, ruling as a designated heir under a male regnal title, is the sharpest index of this flexibility — though it reflects elite practice rather than general female status.

## Temples and learning as economic institutions
- The Thousand-Pillar Temple and Ramappa employed priests, dancers, musicians, garland-makers and cooks, functioning as redistribution centres. In coastal Andhra, Draksharama, Chebrolu and Tripurantakam played the same role.
- The Malkapuram inscription (1261 CE) records endowments creating a matha with teaching halls, a hospital and a rest-house — evidence that Kakatiya surplus was routed into welfare and education, not consumption alone.

## Conclusion

The Kakatiya achievement was integrative rather than merely extractive: they linked a hydraulic interior to a chartered coast and let military service function as a ladder of mobility. That fusion explains both their prosperity and their fragility — the very service elites the system created became the successor Reddi and Velama states after 1323. The template survives in AP's tank-fed tracts and in Telangana's Mission Kakatiya, which consciously invoked it.

## Value addition
- UNESCO: The Kakatiya Rudreswara (Ramappa) Temple, Palampet, was inscribed on the World Heritage List in 2021. India's total stands at 45 World Heritage properties as of July 2026.
- ASI: Kakatiya-period monuments in Andhra Pradesh — including temples at Chebrolu (Guntur) — figure among ASI's centrally protected monuments under the Amaravati Circle, the circle responsible for AP.
- Epigraphic anchors to quote by name: Motupalli Abhaya Sasanam (1244–45, Ganapatideva); Malkapuram inscription (1261, education and hospital endowment); Bayyaram tank inscription (1219, dynastic genealogy). A second, Tamil-and-Grantha inscription of Prataparudra dated 1308 CE was documented at Motupalli and verified by the ASI Epigraphy Branch, Mysuru — proof that the site remains archaeologically live.
- Adopt a Heritage 2.0 (Ministry of Culture / ASI, relaunched 2023) enables CSR-funded visitor amenities at Monuments of National Importance — the policy route through which sites such as Motupalli and Chebrolu can be developed.
- Gyan Bharatam Mission (Rs. 482.85 crore, 2024–31) is digitising manuscript wealth; the National Manuscript Survey launched 16 March 2026 is the vehicle for locating unpublished Kakatiya-period Telugu and Sanskrit material still in private and temple custody.

## Introduction

The Qutb Shahis (1518–1687) ruled a kingdom whose court language was Persian, whose faith was Shia Islam and whose revenue and manpower were overwhelmingly Telugu and Hindu. Composite culture at Golconda was the working solution to that mismatch — visible in a bilingual literary court, a hybrid building idiom, a Telugu scribal administration and an endowment policy that crossed religious lines.

## A court that operated in three languages
- Ibrahim Quli Qutb Shah (1550–80) spent his exile years at Vijayanagara and returned steeped in Telugu court culture; Telugu poets addressed him as Malkibharama. Under him Addanki Gangadhara Kavi composed Tapati-Samvaranopakhyanam and Ponnaganti Telaganarya wrote Yayaticharitra — notable as an achcha-Telugu work deliberately avoiding Sanskrit vocabulary. That a Persianate sultan's court produced a purist Telugu experiment is the strongest single proof of genuine synthesis.
- Muhammad Quli Qutb Shah (1580–1612) compiled the earliest substantial diwan in Dakhni, whose diction absorbs Telugu words, local seasons, festivals and place-names — language contact recorded in verse rather than merely asserted.

## Architecture as visible hybridity
- Charminar (1591) was raised as Muhammad Quli founded Hyderabad. Its four minarets and arches are Islamic in vocabulary, but the lotus-petal medallions, brackets and stucco foliage are executed by local craft traditions — the same masons who carved temples.
- The Qutb Shahi Tombs combine Persian onion domes with lotus-bud finials and kalasa-like crowning members; Golconda Fort is a Kakatiya foundation extended by the dynasty; Purana Pul (1578) and the Badshahi Ashurkhana (1594) add civic and ritual dimensions. In Andhra Pradesh, the dynasty made significant additions to Gandikota Fort.

## Administration staffed across the religious divide
- Akkanna and Madanna, Brahmin brothers of Hanamkonda, controlled the exchequer and revenue administration under Tana Shah. Below them, the Telugu karanam scribal class kept village accounts, which meant the everyday language of governance in the countryside remained Telugu even where the chancery worked in Persian.
- Their execution in 1686, under Mughal pressure precisely because Hindus held such power, shows both how far the accommodation went and how contested it was.

## Endowments and performance traditions
- The dynasty made revenue assignments to Bhadrachalam; Kancharla Gopanna (Ramadasu), Madanna's nephew, served as its revenue officer and his kirtanas entered the Telugu devotional canon.
- Abul Hasan Tana Shah's grant of Kuchipudi village (c. 1675–78) as an agraharam to the Bhagavata Brahmin families secured the material base of a Telugu dance-drama tradition that is today one of India's recognised classical dance forms — the most durable single legacy of Qutb Shahi patronage.

## Commerce as the solvent
- Golconda's diamond wealth came from the Kollur mines in the Krishna valley of present Andhra Pradesh, and its exports moved through Masulipatnam, where Dutch and English factories were established in the early seventeenth century. A port town of Persian, Armenian, Dutch, English and Telugu merchants made cosmopolitanism a daily habit rather than a court ideal.

## Conclusion

Composite culture at Golconda was therefore structural, not merely sentimental: it grew from the practical necessity of taxing, recruiting and building among a population the rulers did not share a faith or language with. Its finest products — a purist Telugu kavya written under a Shia sultan, and a Telugu dance village endowed by the last Qutb Shah — outlived the dynasty itself and remain part of the living cultural inheritance of both Telugu states.

## Value addition
- Ministry of Culture:Kuchipudi is among India's recognised classical dance forms, and its institutional survival is traceable to the Qutb Shahi land grant — a rare, exam-friendly instance of a medieval sannad producing a present-day national art form.
- Telugu classical status (2008) under the Ministry of Culture rests partly on the continuity of literary production through periods such as this; India now recognises 11 classical languages after the Cabinet decision of 3 October 2024.
- ASI / Adopt a Heritage 2.0 (relaunched 2023) covers visitor amenities at Monuments of National Importance; Qutb Shahi-period structures and Gandikota Fort in AP fall within this policy space.
- UNESCO Tentative List: India's list stands at 69 properties; Andhra Pradesh entries include Lepakshi (submitted 17 February 2022), Erra Matti Dibbalu and the Natural Heritage of Tirumala Hills. Gandikota's inclusion has been formally pressed with the Union Tourism and Culture Ministry.
- Correction worth stating in the exam: attribute the mosque-building programme accurately — Mecca Masjid was begun under Muhammad Quli and completed only in the Mughal period; the Shaikpet Sarai, Hayat Bakshi Mosque and Taramati Baradari illustrate the dynasty's civic architecture.
