- Correction — in Andhra Pradesh these soils are derived largely from lime-rich Cuddapah shales and

limestone and from weathered gneiss, not from Deccan Trap basalt. Trap basalt is confined to a small north-western fringe of the state. Writing "weathered from Deccan lava" is the standard mistake in this answer and the examiner notices it, because it is a Maharashtra explanation transplanted to Andhra.

## Physical characteristics
- Deep black to dark brown, from iron and titanium compounds combined with humus, not from high organic content.
- Very high clay fraction of the swelling montmorillonite type, giving high shrink–swell capacity. The soil swells and seals when wet and cracks widely when dry.
- Those cracks are agriculturally decisive: they carry the surface layer downward and turn the profile over, which is why regur is called self-ploughing and why it sustains rain-fed crops through long dry spells on stored moisture alone.

## Chemical characteristics
- Rich in lime, iron, magnesia, alumina and potash; deficient in nitrogen, phosphorus and organic matter.
- High cation exchange capacity, and a neutral to slightly alkaline reaction, which is why nutrient response is good but drainage-induced alkalinity is a standing risk.

## Distribution and crops
- Kurnool, Nandyal, Guntur, Palnadu, Prakasam and parts of Anantapuram.
- Cotton, chilli, turmeric, tobacco, jowar and gram. The Guntur–Palnadu black soil tract underlies India's largest chilli market at Guntur; Kurnool's irrigated black soils under the Tungabhadra system carry cotton and sunflower.

## Alluvial soils

## Origin and parent material
- Transported soils, deposited by the Krishna, Godavari and Penna. Because deposition is continuous, the profile is geologically young and constantly renewed — the source of their fertility.

## Physical characteristics
- Light grey to ash brown; loamy to sandy loam, with clay loams in the older delta interiors.
- Stratified rather than horizoned, because each flood lays a fresh layer; profiles are deep, easily worked and moderately drained — ideal for intensive multiple cropping.

## Chemical characteristics
- Rich in potash and lime, moderately supplied with phosphate, deficient in nitrogen and organic carbon.
- Reaction near neutral. Micronutrient deficiency, particularly zinc, is widespread — a general feature of Andhra soils rather than of the deltas alone.

## Distribution and crops
- The Krishna, Godavari and Penna basins and deltas — Konaseema, East and West Godavari, Krishna, Guntur, Bapatla and Nellore.
- Paddy, sugarcane, banana, coconut, oil palm and vegetables, supported by the Dowleswaram anicut on the Godavari and the Prakasam barrage on the Krishna, which together made this one of India's most productive agro-ecosystems.

## Degradation — the point that converts description into evaluation
- Black soils: waterlogging where canal irrigation has been introduced without drainage; salinity and alkalinity build-up; sheet and gully erosion on the Rayalaseema slopes and ravines along the Penna.
- Alluvial soils: salinity and sodicity along the delta margins, worsened by aquaculture effluent in Krishna, Guntur and Nellore; declining organic carbon under continuous paddy; and loss of fertile deltaic land to urban and industrial conversion.

## Conclusion

The two soils are the physical basis of the state's dual agrarian economy. Black soils allow a rain-fed system in a semi-arid interior, because their moisture retention substitutes for irrigation; alluvial soils allow an intensive irrigated system in the deltas, because continuous deposition substitutes for fertility management. Both are now under stress from the same source — water applied or withheld in the wrong quantity, producing alkalinity in one and salinity in the other. Soil health card based nutrient management, drainage alongside irrigation, zinc and organic carbon correction, and the state's natural farming programme are therefore not soil-conservation extras but the condition for sustaining output.

## Value addition
- The correct shares, worth memorising in order: red about 65 per cent, black about 25, alluvial about 5, laterite about 3, coastal sandy about 2. Mnemonic: Red > Black > Alluvial > Laterite > Sandy. Reject the 30 per cent alluvial figure that circulates in coaching material — alluvium is confined to two delta tracts and cannot approach a third of the state.
- The general deficiency across Andhra Pradesh is zinc, with nitrogen and organic carbon widely low. Naming zinc specifically signals familiarity with state soil survey findings rather than generic textbook content.
- Laterite and sandy soils, in one line each for a fuller answer if time allows: laterite forms by intense leaching in the high-rainfall Eastern Ghats of North Andhra and at Sullurpeta and Kavali, hardens on exposure and is quarried as brick, and carries cashew and plantation crops; coastal sandy soils are saline and highly permeable and support casuarina and cashew shelter belts.
- Conservation measures to close on: contour bunding and contour ploughing on plateau slopes, terracing in the agency areas, check dams and percolation tanks, casuarina shelter belts along the coast, green manuring and crop rotation, and the state's community managed natural farming programme.

## Introduction

Natural endowment decides what a farmer can grow; institutions decide what he will grow. Soil, rainfall and temperature fix the outer boundary of the choice set, but land rights, credit, assured price and market access determine which point inside that boundary is chosen — because each of them changes how much downside risk the household is able to absorb. That is why agro-climatically similar tracts across India carry visibly different cropping patterns.

## How Institutions Control the Cropping Decision
- Land tenure and the investment horizon. A crop choice is an investment decision with a payback period. An oral tenant with a one-season understanding cannot recover the cost of a mango orchard or an oil-palm stand that yields only from the fourth year, so he rationally chooses a short-duration subsistence crop even on land perfectly suited to horticulture. Illustration: tenancy in coastal Andhra Pradesh is widespread and largely unrecorded; the Andhra Pradesh Crop Cultivator Rights Act exists precisely to give such cultivators a documented identity for credit and insurance.
- Credit as the purchase of risk-bearing capacity. Hybrid seed, fertiliser and plant protection must be paid for months before any revenue arrives. Without institutional credit the farmer either scales down inputs or borrows informally at rates that make a single crop failure ruinous, so he defaults to the low-input, low-return crop. Illustration: the Kisan Credit Card limit was raised from Rs.3 lakh to Rs.5 lakh in Budget 2025–26, covering around 7.7 crore farmers, fishers and dairy farmers — a change in the permissible scale of risk, not merely in liquidity.
- Assured price and procurement as a distortion. MSP backed by actual procurement converts a risky crop into a near-riskless one, and farmers respond to that certainty even against agro-climatic logic. Illustration: the Punjab– Haryana wheat–paddy monoculture persists on a falling water table because procurement is assured there, while pulses and oilseeds — better suited and nominally covered by MSP — attract far weaker procurement and therefore far weaker acreage. This is the strongest single evidence for the proposition in the question.
- Irrigation institutions, not just irrigation. A canal creates potential; a Water Users’ Association decides whether the tail-ender receives water. Where distribution is unreliable, the head-reach farmer plants paddy and the tail-ender a dryland crop on identical soil — the institution, not the geography, produces the difference.
- Markets, storage and perishability. Absent cold chain and assured buyers, farmers avoid high-value perishables and retreat to storable, low-value grain. Illustration: Guntur’s mirchi yard — Asia’s largest chilli market — sustains a chilli belt across Guntur, Palnadu and Prakasam that no soil map alone would predict, because the market yard guarantees a buyer.

## Where the Proposition Must Be Qualified
- Institutions bind, but do not override, agro-climate. No credit line will grow paddy in Anantapuramu’s 550 mm regime. Institutions select within the feasible set; they do not enlarge it.
- Institutional reach is itself uneven. Rain-fed eastern India has had weak procurement and thin credit penetration, so the institutions that shaped Punjab’s cropping barely touched Bihar’s — institutional absence is as causally powerful as its presence. And institutions can lock in unsustainable patterns, as groundwater depletion under assured procurement shows.

## Conclusion

The proposition holds, but as a statement about selection rather than determination. Within the envelope set by nature, institutions decide the outcome — and because they do, cropping patterns are policy-responsive in a way soil and rainfall are not. That is the constructive implication: recording tenancy, widening procurement beyond rice and wheat, and building market infrastructure for perishables would shift cropping patterns faster and at lower cost than any further expansion of irrigation.

## Value addition
- PM Dhan-Dhaanya Krishi Yojana (Cabinet 16 July 2025; launched 11 October 2025) is the clearest current admission that the binding constraint is institutional: it converges 36 schemes across 11 ministries in 100 districts chosen for low productivity, low cropping intensity and low credit penetration, at Rs.24,000 crore a year for six years, monitored on 117 KPIs with district plans reviewed by NITI Aayog.
- Diversification missions — Mission for Aatmanirbharta in Pulses (tur, urad, masoor, with assured procurement) and the National Mission on High Yielding Seeds — attack the MSP-induced monoculture directly, by attaching procurement certainty to the crops that lack it.
- Scale of the tenure problem: over 86 per cent of Indian farmers are small and marginal, and average operational holding in Andhra Pradesh has fallen to about 0.94 hectares — fragmentation is what makes institutional support decisive rather than optional.
- Andhra Pradesh example of an institution creating a crop: APCNF, through community institutions and women’s SHGs, moved 17.7 lakh farmers to chemical-free cultivation without any change in soil or rainfall — institutional design alone altered the input regime across 9.2 lakh hectares.
Q92:
## Introduction

India’s irrigation problem has long been one of delivery rather than creation: large storages were built, but water never reached the field channels below the outlet. The Command Area Development Programme, launched in 1974–75 and restructured as CADWM from 1 April 2004, was designed to close that gap between irrigation potential created and potential utilised. Because the unutilised gap was concentrated in backward and drought-prone commands, closing it was inherently a regional-equity instrument — which is exactly why its uneven record matters.

## Why CADP Was Structurally Pro-Equity
- It works below the outlet, where inequality actually lives. Field channels, land levelling, warabandi rotation and drainage determine whether the tail-end farmer receives water at all. Head-reach farmers capture canal water by gravity and position; on-farm development is the only intervention that redistributes within a command rather than merely adding to it. This is the programme’s real equity claim.
- It targeted the commands with the widest unutilised gap. Those were disproportionately in semi-arid and backward tracts, so the same rupee bought more additional irrigated area there than in an already-efficient command — a built-in regional bias in favour of the lagging region.
- Participatory Irrigation Management institutionalised the shift, moving rationing from bureaucratic discretion to a rule-bound rotation and protecting the farmer with least political weight.
- Demonstrated gains. In the Nagarjunasagar and Tungabhadra commands, field-channel development and levelling stabilised paddy and cotton in tracts that had previously cropped only in good years — converting an intermittent crop into an annual one, which changes household income rather than merely yield.

## Why the Equity Promise Has Been Only Partly Realised
- Absorption, not allocation, is the binding constraint — the Andhra evidence. Andhra Pradesh currently has seven CADWM projects with a total approved cost of Rs.971.42 crore at 50 per cent central share, covering a Cultivable Command Area of 1,78,620 hectares. Yet the Socio-Economic Survey 2025–26 records that no physical progress was achieved in any of the seven projects between 1 April and 31 December 2025, against a budget provision of Rs.14.26 crore. A programme that cannot spend cannot equalise — this single datum is worth more than a paragraph of generalised criticism.
- Fiscal capacity biases outcomes toward richer states. A 50 per cent matching requirement means the state best able to find its share draws the most central assistance — partially inverting the equity intent.
- On-farm works decay without maintenance, and where WUAs exist only on paper, or head-reach farmers dominate the committee, PIM reproduces the inequality it was meant to correct.

## The 2025 Redesign and Whether It Answers the Diagnosis
- M-CADWM, approved by the Union Cabinet in April 2025 as a sub-scheme of PMKSY for 2025–26 with an initial outlay of Rs.1,600 crore, shifts the model from open field channels to underground pressurised piped irrigation up to one hectare at the farm gate, with SCADA and IoT-based water accounting.
- Why piping is an equity instrument. A closed pipe cannot be tapped mid-course and delivers at pressure regardless of position in the command — it removes the physical basis of head-reach advantage, which decades of warabandi rules could not.
- Sustainability design. Irrigation Management Transfer to Water User Societies, with five years of handholding and

FPO or PACS linkage, addresses the maintenance failure that eroded earlier gains.

- The caveat. M-CADWM is currently a pilot on challenge funding; the full National Plan begins only from April 2026, aligned with the Sixteenth Finance Commission period, so its equity record is still unwritten.

## Conclusion

CADP correctly identified that India’s irrigation inequality lies below the outlet, not above the dam, and where it was implemented it genuinely converted uncertain cultivation into assured cultivation. Its failure has been one of absorptive and institutional capacity rather than of design — as Andhra Pradesh’s stalled seven projects demonstrate. M-CADWM’s move to piped delivery and transferred asset management addresses that failure at the right point, but the verdict must remain provisional until the national plan from April 2026 produces its own performance record.

## Value addition
- M-CADWM in one line each: PMKSY sub-scheme, Cabinet approval April 2025, Rs.1,600 crore initial outlay for 2025– 26; underground pressurised piped irrigation to the farm gate up to 1 ha; SCADA and IoT water accounting; Irrigation Management Transfer to Water User Societies with five years of support and FPO/PACS linkage; pilots by challenge funding, national plan from April 2026 under the Sixteenth Finance Commission.
- Andhra Pradesh — the examinable numbers: 7 CADWM projects, Rs.971.42 crore approved, CCA 1,78,620 ha, 50 per cent central share; Rs.69.18 crore released by MoWR; nil physical progress April–December 2025.
- Complementary AP interventions: APILIP-II (JICA-assisted, Rs.2,000 crore) has modernised 4 medium projects and 107 MI tanks, stabilising 31,776 ha including 11,017 ha of gap ayacut; the AP Integrated Irrigation and Agriculture Transformation Project (World Bank) targets 400 tanks and 1,12,546 acres for 55,000 families.
- The scale of the stakes: Andhra Pradesh recorded 11.91 lakh minor irrigation sources in the 6th MI Census (2017–18), a 12.96 per cent rise over 2013–14; the 7th MI Census with reference year 2023–24 was 95 per cent enumerated by late 2025.
